lessons.title: The RAAS and Diuretics: Core Antihypertensives
body: Blood pressure is cardiac output times systemic vascular resistance, and every antihypertensive lowers one of those two terms, often by acting on the kidney or the sympathetic nervous system. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) is the largest target. Juxtaglomerular cells release renin when perfusion falls or beta-1 stimulation rises. Renin cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE, abundant in lung endothelium) converts that to angiotensin II, and angiotensin II acting on AT1 receptors constricts arterioles, constricts the efferent arteriole of the glomerulus, releases aldosterone and ADH, and promotes sodium retention and cardiac remodeling.

ACE inhibitors (lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril) block angiotensin II formation. ACE is also kininase II, which degrades bradykinin, so ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin and cause two characteristic class effects: a dry cough in a meaningful minority of patients and, rarely, angioedema. Other toxicities are hyperkalemia (less aldosterone), a rise in creatinine from efferent dilation, and first-dose hypotension in volume-depleted patients. They are contraindicated in pregnancy because second and third trimester exposure causes fetal renal injury and oligohydramnios, and caution is needed in bilateral renal artery stenosis, where glomerular filtration depends on angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole. Angiotensin receptor blockers (losartan, valsartan) block AT1 directly, do not raise bradykinin, and so avoid cough and mostly avoid angioedema, but share the hyperkalemia, pregnancy and renal cautions. Combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB adds hyperkalemia and kidney injury without proven benefit, and ACE inhibitors must never be combined with sacubitril-valsartan because neprilysin inhibition plus ACE inhibition risks angioedema.

Diuretics are best learned by nephron segment. Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide) block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, are the most powerful natriuretics, and cause hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia and dose-related ototoxicity. Thiazides (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone) block the sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, and uniquely reduce urinary calcium excretion, so they cause hypercalcemia and can help calcium kidney stones. Their other effects are hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia, hyperglycemia and hyperlipidemia. The ALLHAT trial supported thiazide-type diuretics as an excellent first-line choice. Potassium-sparing agents act on the collecting duct: amiloride and triamterene block the epithelial sodium channel, while spironolactone and eplerenone block the mineralocorticoid receptor. All raise potassium; spironolactone also blocks androgen and progesterone receptors, giving gynecomastia and menstrual irregularity that the more selective eplerenone largely avoids.

The 2025 AHA/ACC hypertension guideline (which replaced the 2017 version and uses the PREVENT risk equations to guide treatment) treats thiazide-type diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers as first-line classes for most adults. Worked example: a patient with hypertension, type 2 diabetes and albuminuria is best served by an ACE inhibitor or ARB because blocking efferent constriction lowers glomerular pressure and slows nephropathy. If that patient develops a dry cough, switching to an ARB keeps the benefit while removing the bradykinin effect.

lessons.title: Calcium Channel Blockers, Beta Blockers, Vasodilators and Nitrates
body: Calcium channel blockers inhibit L-type voltage-gated calcium channels, and the two subclasses differ in where they bind best. Dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine) prefer vascular smooth muscle, so they are potent arterial vasodilators with little effect on conduction. Their adverse effects follow from vasodilation: flushing, headache, reflex tachycardia (especially short-acting nifedipine) and peripheral edema that comes from precapillary dilation and does not respond to diuretics. The non-dihydropyridines (verapamil, diltiazem) prefer the heart: they slow sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodal conduction and reduce contractility, which makes them useful for rate control in atrial fibrillation and supraventricular tachycardia but dangerous in combination with beta blockers, in decompensated systolic heart failure and in advanced AV block. Verapamil classically causes constipation and inhibits CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, raising digoxin levels.

Beta blockers antagonize beta-adrenergic receptors. Beta-1 blockade lowers heart rate, contractility and renin release, which reduces myocardial oxygen demand; this is why they relieve angina and improve survival after myocardial infarction and in chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Cardioselective agents (metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol) are safer in asthma and diabetes than nonselective agents (propranolol, nadolol), whose beta-2 blockade can provoke bronchospasm, blunt recovery from hypoglycemia, and worsen peripheral vasoconstriction. Carvedilol and labetalol also block alpha-1 and so vasodilate; nebivolol adds nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation. Hallmark toxicities are bradycardia, AV block, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and in abrupt withdrawal a rebound surge of tachycardia and ischemia because receptors have upregulated. In cocaine toxicity, unopposed alpha stimulation is a theoretical concern with pure beta blockade. Beta blockers with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity are not preferred after infarction.

Direct vasodilators act on smooth muscle. Hydralazine opens arterioles through mechanisms involving nitric oxide and cyclic GMP, causing reflex tachycardia, fluid retention and a drug-induced lupus syndrome, especially in slow acetylators; it is used in hypertensive emergencies of pregnancy and, with isosorbide dinitrate, in heart failure in self-identified Black patients (A-HeFT). Minoxidil opens potassium channels, causes marked reflex tachycardia, salt retention and hypertrichosis. Nitrates (nitroglycerin, isosorbide mononitrate) are denitrated to release nitric oxide, raising cyclic GMP in vascular smooth muscle. They dilate veins far more than arteries at low doses, which reduces preload and wall tension, so oxygen demand falls; they also dilate epicardial coronary arteries. Toxicities are headache, hypotension and tolerance with continuous exposure, which is why a nitrate-free interval is built into schedules. Because sildenafil and other PDE5 inhibitors block cyclic GMP breakdown, combining them with nitrates can produce profound hypotension, a classic absolute contraindication.

Worked example: a man with stable angina takes a long-acting nitrate and is prescribed sildenafil. The two synergize on cyclic GMP and the result may be a precipitous fall in blood pressure and myocardial hypoperfusion. The correct decision is to avoid the combination, not to lower either dose.

lessons.title: Heart Failure Pharmacotherapy and Digoxin
body: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) is a vicious cycle: a weak ventricle lowers perfusion, which activates the sympathetic nervous system and RAAS, which raises preload and afterload and drives remodeling and further pump failure. Drugs that interrupt this neurohormonal loop reduce mortality; drugs that only relieve congestion improve symptoms. The 2022 ACC/AHA/HFSA guideline organizes therapy around four foundational classes for HFrEF.

First, inhibition of the RAAS: ACE inhibitors or ARBs, and preferably the angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor sacubitril-valsartan, which beat enalapril in PARADIGM-HF. Neprilysin degrades natriuretic peptides and bradykinin, so blocking it raises vasodilatory natriuretic peptides; this is also why combining sacubitril with an ACE inhibitor is contraindicated, and why a washout is required when switching. Second, evidence-based beta blockers (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol), started low in stable patients because acute negative inotropy can worsen decompensation. Third, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone), shown to reduce mortality in RALES and EPHESUS, with hyperkalemia monitoring. Fourth, SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin), which reduced heart failure hospitalization and cardiovascular death in DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced even in patients without diabetes, though the exact mechanism is still debated.

Loop diuretics treat congestion but have no demonstrated mortality benefit. Hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate is added in self-identified Black patients with persistent symptoms (A-HeFT) and in those who cannot take RAAS inhibitors. Ivabradine inhibits the funny current (If) in the sinus node, lowering heart rate without negative inotropy, and is used for patients in sinus rhythm with a persistently elevated rate despite a maximal beta blocker; its notable toxicities are visual phosphenes and bradycardia. Drugs to avoid in HFrEF include non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, thiazolidinediones, which cause fluid retention, and most NSAIDs.

Digoxin inhibits the Na+/K+-ATPase of cardiac myocytes. Intracellular sodium rises, the sodium-calcium exchanger extrudes less calcium, and contractility increases; it also augments vagal tone, slowing AV conduction. It improves symptoms and lowers hospitalization but not mortality, and has a narrow therapeutic window. Toxicity produces nausea, visual changes with yellow-green halos, hyperkalemia in acute overdose, and arrhythmias including atrial tachycardia with block and ventricular ectopy. Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia increase the risk. Interactions with quinidine, amiodarone, verapamil and clarithromycin raise levels because of P-glycoprotein inhibition and reduced renal clearance. Digoxin-specific antibody fragments are the antidote.

Worked example: an ejection fraction of 30 percent with edema and a heart rate of 90 in sinus rhythm calls for a loop diuretic for the congestion plus all four foundational classes titrated as tolerated. Adding digoxin is a later, symptom-driven option rather than a mortality strategy.

lessons.title: Antiarrhythmic Drugs
body: Antiarrhythmic drugs change ion currents so as to suppress abnormal automaticity, triggered activity or reentry. The Vaughan Williams scheme sorts them by dominant effect on the cardiac action potential, and its central lesson is that nearly every drug that corrects one rhythm can provoke another, so drug choice depends on the substrate and on structural heart disease.

Class I drugs block fast sodium channels, slowing phase 0 depolarization and conduction. They are use-dependent, working more at fast rates. Class IA (quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide) also block potassium channels, prolonging the action potential and QT; they cause torsades de pointes, and procainamide causes drug-induced lupus. Class IB (lidocaine, mexiletine) bind preferentially to depolarized, ischemic tissue and shorten the action potential, so they are used for ventricular arrhythmias, especially after infarction or in digoxin toxicity, and cause neurotoxicity such as paresthesia and seizures. Class IC (flecainide, propafenone) are the strongest sodium blockers with little effect on repolarization; the CAST trial showed they increased mortality after myocardial infarction, so they are contraindicated in structural heart disease or ischemic heart disease.

Class II is beta blockade, which slows the sinus node and AV node and is useful for rate control and for reducing sudden death after infarction. Class III drugs block potassium channels and prolong repolarization and refractoriness: sotalol (also a nonselective beta blocker), dofetilide, ibutilide and amiodarone. Pure potassium channel blockers risk QT prolongation and torsades de pointes, and are therefore started in monitored settings with renal function in mind. Amiodarone is unusual because it also blocks sodium, calcium and beta receptors. It is highly effective but accumulates in tissue with an extremely long half-life, and its toxicities include pulmonary fibrosis, hepatotoxicity, hypo- or hyperthyroidism because of its iodine content, corneal microdeposits, photosensitivity with blue-gray skin discoloration, and bradycardia. It inhibits CYP enzymes and P-glycoprotein, raising warfarin and digoxin effects. Baseline and periodic thyroid, liver and pulmonary monitoring follow from this profile.

Class IV drugs are the non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, which slow AV nodal conduction. Adenosine is outside the classification but is a first-line pharmacologic termination for AV nodal reentrant tachycardia: it activates A1 receptors and potassium conductance, producing a brief AV block. Its effect lasts seconds, and it can cause transient flushing, chest tightness and bronchospasm; methylxanthines such as caffeine and theophylline antagonize it, while dipyridamole potentiates it. Magnesium sulfate is the treatment for torsades de pointes, alongside correcting hypokalemia and stopping QT-prolonging drugs.

Worked example: a patient with prior myocardial infarction and scar develops frequent premature ventricular beats. Flecainide, though effective at suppressing the beats, is the wrong choice because ischemic and scarred myocardium turns sodium channel blockade into a substrate for fatal reentry.

lessons.title: Lipid-Lowering Agents
body: Atherosclerosis is driven by apolipoprotein B-containing particles, chiefly LDL, retained in the arterial wall, so most lipid drugs aim to lower LDL cholesterol or, for triglycerides, to lower very-low-density lipoprotein production or speed its clearance. The hepatocyte is the key site: it makes cholesterol in a pathway whose rate-limiting step is HMG-CoA reductase, and it clears LDL from blood through LDL receptors that are recycled or degraded under control of the protein PCSK9.

Statins (atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, simvastatin, pravastatin) competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase. The fall in hepatic cholesterol activates SREBP-2, which upregulates LDL receptors, and LDL falls substantially. Statins reduced cardiovascular events and death in the Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study (4S) and many later trials, and the 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline (which replaced the 2018 cholesterol guideline) keeps them as the foundation of treatment, bases primary-prevention decisions on PREVENT-estimated risk, restores LDL cholesterol goals (below 70 mg/dL in high-risk patients and below 55 mg/dL for very-high-risk secondary prevention), and adds nonstatin drugs such as ezetimibe, bempedoic acid or a PCSK9 monoclonal antibody when goals are not reached. Their toxicities are myopathy (myalgias, sometimes rhabdomyolysis with creatine kinase elevation), dose-related transaminase elevation, and a small increase in new-onset diabetes. Most patients stop a statin once pregnancy is recognized, but the FDA removed the blanket pregnancy contraindication in 2021 so that very-high-risk patients can weigh benefit and risk individually; breastfeeding on a statin is still not advised. Interactions determine most serious muscle toxicity: simvastatin and lovastatin are cleared by CYP3A4, so strong inhibitors such as clarithromycin, azole antifungals, protease inhibitors

and large amounts of grapefruit juice raise levels; gemfibrozil inhibits statin glucuronidation and raises levels of several statins; cyclosporine inhibits the OATP1B1 uptake transporter. Pravastatin and rosuvastatin undergo little CYP metabolism.

Ezetimibe blocks the NPC1L1 sterol transporter at the intestinal brush border, lowering cholesterol absorption and adding a modest further LDL reduction; it is well tolerated. PCSK9 inhibitors (the monoclonal antibodies evolocumab and alirocumab, and the small interfering RNA inclisiran) prevent LDL receptor degradation, so more receptors recycle to the surface and LDL falls sharply; they are used in very high-risk patients or familial hypercholesterolemia not at goal on statins. Bempedoic acid inhibits ATP-citrate lyase upstream of HMG-CoA reductase and can raise uric acid and risk tendon rupture. Bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colesevelam) bind bile acids in the gut, depleting hepatic cholesterol, but can raise triglycerides, cause bloating and bind other drugs, so they are given apart from them.

For triglyceride-predominant disease, fibrates (gemfibrozil, fenofibrate) activate PPAR-alpha, increasing lipoprotein lipase and lowering VLDL; they cause myopathy with statins (more with gemfibrozil) and gallstones. Niacin lowers LDL and triglycerides and raises HDL, causes prostaglandin-mediated flushing, hyperuricemia and hyperglycemia, and has not shown added cardiovascular benefit on top of statins in trials. Icosapent ethyl, a purified omega-3 ester, lowered events in REDUCE-IT in patients with elevated triglycerides on statins, but benefit is not shown for all omega-3 products.

Worked example: a man on simvastatin begins clarithromycin for pneumonia and develops dark urine and muscle pain. CYP3A4 inhibition has raised simvastatin exposure and rhabdomyolysis is likely, so the statin must be stopped and creatine kinase and renal function checked.

lessons.title: Antiplatelets, Anticoagulants and Fibrinolytics
body: Thrombi in arteries are platelet-rich and are prevented mainly with antiplatelet drugs; thrombi in veins and the heart are fibrin-rich and are prevented mainly with anticoagulants. Knowing the target in each pathway predicts the toxicities, the monitoring and the antidote.

Aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclooxygenase-1, preventing platelet thromboxane A2 synthesis for the platelet lifetime because platelets cannot make new enzyme. Toxicities include gastrointestinal bleeding, Reye syndrome in children with viral illness, and bronchospasm in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease. Clopidogrel, prasugrel and ticagrelor block the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor. Clopidogrel and prasugrel are prodrugs: clopidogrel requires CYP2C19, so loss-of-function variants and strong inhibitors such as omeprazole can blunt its effect. Prasugrel is more potent but carries more bleeding and is avoided after prior stroke or transient ischemic attack. Ticagrelor is a reversible, direct-acting inhibitor whose characteristic adverse effects are dyspnea and bradyarrhythmias. Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors (abciximab, eptifibatide) block the final common pathway of aggregation and cause bleeding and thrombocytopenia.

Unfractionated heparin binds antithrombin and accelerates inactivation of thrombin and factor Xa; effect is monitored by activated partial thromboplastin time, it is safe in renal failure and pregnancy, and protamine sulfate reverses it. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is an immune reaction to platelet factor 4-heparin complexes, typically with platelet falls beginning around days 5 to 10 and a paradoxical prothrombotic state; heparin is stopped and a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban is used. Low molecular weight heparins (enoxaparin) preferentially inhibit factor Xa, have predictable pharmacokinetics but renal clearance and incomplete protamine reversal. Fondaparinux is a pure indirect factor Xa inhibitor with very low HIT risk.

Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), preventing gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S. Because protein C has the shortest half-life, early therapy can cause a transient hypercoagulable state with skin necrosis, which is why it overlaps with heparin. It is monitored by the prothrombin time and INR, is teratogenic (warfarin embryopathy), and is affected by CYP2C9 and VKORC1 genetics, by diet vitamin K and by many interactions: inhibitors such as metronidazole, azoles and amiodarone raise the INR, while inducers such as rifampin and carbamazepine lower it. Reversal uses vitamin K, with prothrombin complex concentrate for life-threatening bleeding.

Direct oral anticoagulants include the factor Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban) and the direct thrombin inhibitor dabigatran. They have fixed dosing without routine monitoring and noninferior efficacy for stroke prevention in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, with apixaban showing lower major bleeding than warfarin in ARISTOTLE. They are not appropriate in mechanical heart valves or typically in severe antiphospholipid syndrome. Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran; andexanet alfa or prothrombin complex concentrate reverses factor Xa inhibitors. Fibrinolytics such as alteplase convert plasminogen to plasmin, and cause hemorrhage; contraindications include prior intracranial hemorrhage, recent major surgery or stroke, and active bleeding. Tranexamic acid and aminocaproic acid inhibit plasminogen activation and reduce bleeding.
Worked example: a patient on warfarin starts metronidazole and develops bruising with an INR of 6. CYP2C9 inhibition reduced warfarin clearance, so the antibiotic raised exposure.

lessons.title: Drugs for Diabetes Mellitus
body: Type 2 diabetes combines insulin resistance in liver and muscle with a progressive decline in beta-cell secretion, so drugs work by reducing hepatic glucose output, improving insulin sensitivity, increasing insulin release, mimicking incretins or wasting glucose in urine. Modern guidance, including the ADA Standards of Care, individualizes therapy and favors agents with proven cardiorenal benefit in patients with atherosclerotic disease, heart failure or chronic kidney disease, independent of glycemic control.

Metformin lowers hepatic gluconeogenesis, activating AMP-kinase and inhibiting mitochondrial complex I, and modestly improves peripheral sensitivity. It does not cause hypoglycemia on its own or weight gain, and the UKPDS supported its use in overweight patients. Toxicities are gastrointestinal upset, vitamin B12 deficiency with long use and, rarely, lactic acidosis, which is why it is held with severe renal impairment, hypoxia, sepsis or at the time of iodinated contrast in at-risk patients. Sulfonylureas (glipizide, glimepiride, glyburide) close the beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium channel by binding SUR1, depolarizing the cell and releasing insulin. Hypoglycemia and weight gain are the hallmarks; glyburide is hazardous in older adults and renal impairment because its active metabolites persist. Meglitinides act on the same channel with shorter effect. Thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone) activate PPAR-gamma, improving sensitivity, but cause fluid retention and heart failure, fractures and weight gain, so are avoided in heart failure.

Incretin-based drugs exploit glucose-dependent insulin release. GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide) increase insulin and suppress glucagon in a glucose-dependent way, slow gastric emptying and reduce appetite. Nausea, vomiting and delayed gastric emptying are common, with gallbladder disease and a concern for pancreatitis; they carry a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors and are contraindicated with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2. Liraglutide reduced major cardiovascular events in LEADER, and tirzepatide is a dual GIP and GLP-1 agonist. DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin) block incretin breakdown, are weight-neutral and can cause pancreatitis, joint pain and, for some, heart failure signals.

SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin) block glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule, causing glucosuria and osmotic diuresis. EMPA-REG OUTCOME showed reduced cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalization, and later trials showed kidney protection. Adverse effects are genital mycotic infections, volume depletion, euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis and rare necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum (Fournier gangrene); glycemic efficacy falls as eGFR falls, but cardiorenal benefits persist. Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors (acarbose) delay carbohydrate absorption and cause flatulence.

Insulin remains essential in type 1 diabetes and for advanced type 2 disease. Rapid analogs (lispro, aspart) cover meals, long-acting analogs (glargine, degludec) provide basal coverage. The dose-limiting toxicity is hypoglycemia, with weight gain, lipohypertrophy and, in intravenous therapy, hypokalemia as insulin shifts potassium into cells.

Worked example: a patient with type 2 diabetes, established coronary disease and an eGFR of 40 whose hemoglobin A1c is above goal on metformin benefits from adding an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 agonist for cardiovascular protection rather than another sulfonylurea.

lessons.title: Thyroid Drugs
body: Thyroid hormone synthesis requires iodide uptake by the sodium-iodide symporter, oxidation and attachment to tyrosines on thyroglobulin by thyroid peroxidase (organification), coupling into thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), and release under thyroid-stimulating hormone. T4 is the main product, and peripheral deiodinases convert it to the more active T3. Each drug class interrupts or replaces one of these steps.

Levothyroxine, synthetic T4, is the standard for hypothyroidism because its long half-life gives stable levels and it converts to T3 as needed. It has a narrow therapeutic index and is monitored by TSH. Absorption is reduced by calcium, iron, aluminum antacids, bile acid sequestrants and, to a degree, proton pump inhibitors, so these are separated from it. Hepatic enzyme inducers such as rifampin and carbamazepine raise clearance, and estrogen raises thyroxine-binding globulin, increasing the replacement requirement in pregnancy and with oral estrogens. Overreplacement produces iatrogenic hyperthyroidism with palpitations, atrial fibrillation and bone loss, particularly in postmenopausal women and older adults. Liothyronine (T3) acts quickly but swings the level more.

Thionamides (methimazole, propylthiouracil) inhibit thyroid peroxidase, blocking organification and coupling. They do not stop release of preformed hormone, so effect takes weeks. Propylthiouracil additionally inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to T3, giving a faster fall in T3 in thyroid storm. The most feared toxicity of both is agranulocytosis, which should prompt stopping the drug when fever or sore throat occurs; rash and arthralgia are common. Propylthiouracil carries a boxed warning for fulminant hepatotoxicity and is associated with ANCA-positive vasculitis, so methimazole is preferred except in the first trimester of pregnancy and in thyroid storm. Methimazole in early pregnancy is associated with congenital malformations, including aplasia cutis and choanal atresia. Radioactive iodine-131 is taken up by thyroid tissue and ablates it, producing hypothyroidism that needs replacement; it is avoided in pregnancy and requires caution in moderate-to-severe thyroid eye disease. Surgery is another definitive route.

Beta blockers (propranolol) control the adrenergic symptoms of thyrotoxicosis such as tremor and tachycardia, and propranolol additionally reduces peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion. Large doses of iodide transiently inhibit hormone release and synthesis through the Wolff-Chaikoff effect; potassium iodide is given only after a thionamide in thyroid storm so the iodine does not supply fresh substrate for hormone synthesis. Glucocorticoids also reduce conversion and treat storm.

Drug effects on the thyroid are common test material. Amiodarone, with high iodine content, can cause either hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism. Lithium can cause hypothyroidism and goiter. Interferon alpha and immune checkpoint inhibitors may cause thyroiditis.

Worked example: a woman at eight weeks of pregnancy with Graves disease should generally receive propylthiouracil for the first trimester because of the fetal risk of methimazole, then transition to methimazole afterward to limit hepatotoxicity exposure.

lessons.title: Corticosteroids
body: Glucocorticoids are lipophilic hormones that cross the cell membrane and bind the cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor. The complex moves to the nucleus, where it binds glucocorticoid response elements and changes gene transcription. Two effects matter most in therapy. Transrepression: the complex inhibits transcription factors such as NF-kappa B and AP-1, lowering production of cytokines, adhesion molecules and cyclooxygenase-2. Transactivation: it raises expression of anti-inflammatory proteins, including annexin A1 (lipocortin), which restrains phospholipase A2 and so the arachidonic acid cascade. Because they act on gene expression, effects take hours to appear and persist after the drug is cleared.

The therapeutic effects are broad: reduced inflammation, suppression of T-cell and antibody activity, and stabilization of vascular permeability. A useful laboratory signature is a rise in circulating neutrophils (demargination and reduced apoptosis) with falls in lymphocytes and eosinophils. Indications include asthma and COPD exacerbations, autoimmune and inflammatory disease, transplant rejection, cerebral edema from tumors, adrenal insufficiency, prevention of nausea in chemotherapy, and antenatal betamethasone or dexamethasone to accelerate fetal lung maturation before preterm delivery.

Potency and mineralocorticoid action differ by agent. Hydrocortisone is physiologic cortisol with appreciable mineralocorticoid effect. Prednisone is a prodrug converted by the liver to prednisolone, so prednisolone is used where hepatic conversion may be impaired. Methylprednisolone has little mineralocorticoid action. Dexamethasone is long-acting with the highest anti-inflammatory potency and virtually no mineralocorticoid effect. Fludrocortisone is used for its mineralocorticoid effect, to replace aldosterone in primary adrenal insufficiency, and acts through renal sodium retention and potassium and hydrogen ion excretion.

Toxicity follows from the metabolic and immunologic effects, and is mostly dose and duration related. Hyperglycemia and diabetes arise from gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance. Muscle wasting (proximal myopathy), thin skin, easy bruising, central fat redistribution, hypertension, edema and hypokalemic alkalosis reflect catabolic and mineralocorticoid effects. Osteoporosis and avascular necrosis of the femoral head are important, and bone protection is considered with long courses. Cataracts, raised intraocular pressure, mood changes ranging from euphoria to psychosis, insomnia, peptic ulcer risk especially with NSAIDs, and infection risk, including reactivation of latent tuberculosis, round out the list. Inhaled preparations carry local problems such as oral candidiasis and dysphonia, reduced by rinsing and spacers.

The most testable principle is adrenal suppression. Exogenous glucocorticoid suppresses hypothalamic CRH and pituitary ACTH through negative feedback, and the adrenal cortex atrophies. A patient who has taken a pharmacologic dose for more than a few weeks may not mount a cortisol response to stress, so therapy is tapered rather than stopped abruptly, and stress-dose coverage may be needed during surgery or severe illness. Abrupt withdrawal or serious stress can cause adrenal crisis with hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. In secondary adrenal insufficiency from steroid use the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis remains intact, so mineralocorticoid replacement is not needed, unlike primary adrenal disease.

Worked example: a woman on prednisone for several months for an autoimmune disease stops it on her own and, a week later during influenza, collapses with low blood pressure and sodium. Suppression of the HPA axis explains the failure to produce cortisol in stress, and treatment is intravenous hydrocortisone with fluids.

lessons.title: Respiratory Drugs: Asthma and COPD
body: Asthma and COPD are treated with drugs that relax airway smooth muscle, reduce inflammation, or block specific mediators. Airway smooth muscle tone is raised by parasympathetic muscarinic M3 signaling and lowered by beta-2 adrenergic receptor stimulation, which raises cyclic AMP. Eosinophilic airway inflammation, driven by interleukins 4, 5 and 13 and IgE, accounts for much of asthma.

Short-acting beta-2 agonists (albuterol) give rapid relief. Their adverse effects follow from systemic beta stimulation: tremor, tachycardia, palpitations, and hypokalemia as potassium shifts into cells. Long-acting beta agonists (salmeterol, formoterol) give prolonged bronchodilation but, when used alone in asthma, were linked to increased asthma-related deaths, so they are given only with an inhaled corticosteroid. Inhaled corticosteroids (budesonide, fluticasone) are the cornerstone of persistent asthma because they reduce inflammation, exacerbations and hyperresponsiveness; local effects are oral thrush and hoarseness. The GINA strategy now favors an anti-inflammatory reliever, low-dose inhaled corticosteroid with formoterol, in place of a short-acting beta agonist alone, reflecting the risk of treating symptoms without controlling inflammation.

Anticholinergic bronchodilators block M3 receptors: ipratropium (short-acting) and tiotropium and similar agents (long-acting, LAMA). They are central in COPD, where cholinergic tone is a prominent reversible component, and cause dry mouth, urinary retention and, rarely, angle-closure glaucoma. COPD maintenance usually combines a LAMA with a long-acting beta agonist, with inhaled corticosteroid added for patients with frequent exacerbations and higher eosinophil counts. Roflumilast, a phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor, reduces exacerbations in severe COPD with chronic bronchitis and causes weight loss, nausea and psychiatric effects.

Leukotriene pathway agents block mediators made from arachidonic acid by 5-lipoxygenase. Montelukast and zafirlukast antagonize the cysteinyl leukotriene receptor, helping aspirin-exacerbated and exercise-induced asthma and allergic rhinitis; montelukast carries a boxed warning for neuropsychiatric events. Zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase and is hepatotoxic. Theophylline inhibits phosphodiesterase and antagonizes adenosine; it has a narrow therapeutic window with nausea, tachyarrhythmias and seizures, and clearance is lowered by CYP1A2 inhibitors such as ciprofloxacin and raised by smoking. Cromolyn stabilizes mast cells and has little systemic effect.

Biologics are reserved for severe asthma and are phenotype-matched. Omalizumab binds free IgE and is used in allergic asthma, with a small risk of anaphylaxis. Mepolizumab and reslizumab block interleukin-5, and benralizumab targets its receptor, for eosinophilic asthma. Dupilumab blocks the shared interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 receptor subunit.

Cough preparations are lower yield: dextromethorphan is a central antitussive and an NMDA antagonist that is serotonergic at high doses, and benzonatate is a peripherally acting anesthetic of stretch receptors that is dangerous in pediatric ingestion.

Worked example: a patient with asthma who uses albuterol daily and wakes at night has inflammation not controlled by bronchodilation alone, so the best step is adding a regular inhaled corticosteroid, not increasing albuterol.

lessons.title: Gastrointestinal Drugs
body: The parietal cell secretes acid when stimulated by histamine (H2 receptor), gastrin (CCK-B) and acetylcholine (M3), and the final common step is the hydrogen-potassium ATPase proton pump. Drugs reduce acid by blocking the receptors, the pump, or by neutralization.

Proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole, esomeprazole, pantoprazole) are prodrugs activated in acid that irreversibly bind the pump, so they are most effective when pumps are active, taken before meals. They are first-line for gastroesophageal reflux disease, peptic ulcer, erosive esophagitis, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and gastroprotection in patients on NSAIDs. Long-term associations include Clostridioides difficile infection, community-acquired pneumonia, hypomagnesemia, vitamin B12 and iron malabsorption and fracture risk, and rebound acid hypersecretion on stopping. Omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19, which can blunt clopidogrel activation. H2 blockers (famotidine, ranitidine formerly) are weaker and develop tachyphylaxis; cimetidine inhibits several CYP enzymes and has antiandrogen effects such as gynecomastia. Antacids neutralize acid and cause constipation (aluminum) or diarrhea (magnesium), and chelate other drugs. Sucralfate forms a protective barrier on ulcers in an acid environment and needs separation from other drugs. Misoprostol, a prostaglandin E1 analog, restores mucosal protection against NSAID injury, causes diarrhea and cramps, and is contraindicated in pregnancy because it causes uterine contractions.

Helicobacter pylori eradication relies on combining acid suppression with antibiotics. Because clarithromycin resistance is now common, the American College of Gastroenterology 2024 guideline favors bismuth quadruple therapy (a PPI, bismuth, tetracycline and a nitroimidazole) in many patients, and treatment success is confirmed by testing afterward.

Antiemetics are classified by receptor. Ondansetron blocks 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents and the chemoreceptor trigger zone, is first-line for chemotherapy-induced nausea, and causes constipation, headache and dose-related QT prolongation. Aprepitant and similar drugs block substance P at NK1 receptors for delayed chemotherapy nausea. Metoclopramide blocks D2 receptors and enhances acetylcholine release, so it is a prokinetic for gastroparesis; its boxed warning concerns tardive dyskinesia, and it also causes acute dystonia and akathisia. Phenothiazines such as prochlorperazine block D2 and H1 and add sedation and extrapyramidal effects. Scopolamine (antimuscarinic) and meclizine (H1) treat vestibular nausea.

For bowel disease, mesalamine (5-aminosalicylic acid) acts topically in ulcerative colitis, with rare interstitial nephritis. Loperamide is a peripheral mu-opioid agonist that slows motility with little central effect, but excessive doses can cause arrhythmia. Osmotic laxatives such as polyethylene glycol and lactulose draw water into the lumen; lactulose also acidifies colonic contents, trapping ammonia as ammonium, and treats hepatic encephalopathy, often with the poorly absorbed antibiotic rifaximin. Octreotide, a somatostatin analog, lowers splanchnic flow and is used in variceal bleeding and carcinoid syndrome.

Worked example: a patient on clopidogrel with a stent needs gastroprotection. A PPI with less CYP2C19 inhibition, such as pantoprazole, is preferred over omeprazole because it preserves clopidogrel activation.

lessons.title: NSAIDs, Acetaminophen and Gout Drugs
body: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) inhibit cyclooxygenase, blocking conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandins and thromboxane. COX-1 is constitutive, supporting gastric mucosal protection, platelet thromboxane and renal blood flow; COX-2 is induced at sites of inflammation and also contributes to renal and endothelial prostacyclin. Inhibition produces the therapeutic analgesic, antipyretic and anti-inflammatory effects, and explains the toxicities.

The gastrointestinal toxicity is dyspepsia, ulcers and bleeding because mucosal prostaglandins are lost. The renal toxicity matters: prostaglandins vasodilate the afferent arteriole, so NSAIDs in a patient depending on this compensation, such as someone with volume depletion, heart failure, cirrhosis or chronic kidney disease, cause acute kidney injury, sodium and water retention and hyperkalemia. The combination of an NSAID, a diuretic and an ACE inhibitor or ARB, the so-called triple whammy, is a classic cause of kidney injury. NSAIDs can raise blood pressure, antagonize antihypertensives, and increase cardiovascular thrombotic risk. They cause platelet dysfunction, can precipitate bronchospasm in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, and are avoided in late pregnancy because they may close the ductus arteriosus. Ketorolac is potent and limited to short courses because of bleeding and kidney risk.

COX-2 selective inhibitors (celecoxib) were designed to spare gastric COX-1. They lower ulcer risk but still have renal effects, and rofecoxib was withdrawn in 2004 after increased cardiovascular events. In PRECISION, celecoxib was noninferior to ibuprofen and naproxen for cardiovascular safety. Celecoxib is a sulfonamide, so sulfonamide allergy is a caution, and its inhibition of prostacyclin without blocking platelet thromboxane gives the thrombotic concern. Aspirin has antiplatelet effects at low doses and can cause salicylate toxicity at high doses, with tinnitus, respiratory alkalosis followed by anion-gap acidosis.

Acetaminophen is analgesic and antipyretic with minimal anti-inflammatory action, probably through central COX inhibition. At therapeutic doses it is conjugated safely, but in overdose the saturated pathways shunt drug to CYP2E1, forming N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), which glutathione normally detoxifies. When glutathione is depleted, NAPQI causes centrilobular hepatic necrosis. Chronic alcohol use and fasting increase risk. N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and is the antidote, most effective when started early.

Gout is inflammation caused by monosodium urate crystals. Acute flares are treated with NSAIDs, colchicine or glucocorticoids. Colchicine binds tubulin, preventing microtubule assembly and neutrophil migration; toxicities are diarrhea, myopathy and marrow suppression, magnified by CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibitors such as clarithromycin. Long-term urate lowering uses allopurinol or febuxostat, xanthine oxidase inhibitors. Allopurinol can cause severe cutaneous hypersensitivity linked to HLA-B*58:01, raises levels of azathioprine and mercaptopurine because it blocks their breakdown, and is typically started at a low dose. Febuxostat carries a boxed warning for cardiovascular death from the CARES trial. Probenecid blocks renal urate reabsorption but is avoided in uric acid kidney stones. Pegloticase is an enzyme converting urate to allantoin for refractory gout. Starting urate-lowering therapy can provoke flares, so prophylaxis is given and the drug is not stopped during a flare.

Worked example: an older man on lisinopril and furosemide takes ibuprofen for back pain and presents with a rising creatinine. Loss of prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilation, combined with the other two drugs, reduced glomerular filtration.

lessons.title: Immunosuppressants and Biologic Agents
body: Immunosuppressants prevent transplant rejection and treat autoimmune disease by disabling T cells, B cells or cytokine signaling. All raise the risk of infection and, with longer use, of certain cancers, so the principles of toxicity are shared: opportunistic infection, lymphoma and skin cancer, and drug-specific organ injury.

Calcineurin inhibitors are the backbone of transplant regimens. Cyclosporine binds cyclophilin and tacrolimus binds FKBP12; each complex inhibits calcineurin, a phosphatase that activates NFAT, so interleukin-2 transcription and T-cell activation fall. Both cause nephrotoxicity from afferent vasoconstriction, hypertension, hyperkalemia and neurotoxicity such as tremor; cyclosporine adds gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism, while tacrolimus more often causes new-onset diabetes. Both are metabolized by CYP3A4 and have narrow therapeutic windows, so inhibitors such as azole antifungals and macrolides raise toxicity while rifampin lowers levels and risks rejection. Sirolimus also binds FKBP12 but inhibits mTOR, blocking IL-2 signaling and T-cell proliferation; it is less nephrotoxic but causes hyperlipidemia, impaired wound healing, cytopenias and mouth ulcers, and is used in drug-eluting stents.

Antimetabolites interfere with lymphocyte proliferation. Mycophenolate mofetil is converted to mycophenolic acid, inhibiting inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase and so guanine nucleotide synthesis, which lymphocytes cannot bypass; its toxicities are gastrointestinal upset, marrow suppression and teratogenicity. Azathioprine is a prodrug of 6-mercaptopurine, which is inactivated by thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) and xanthine oxidase. TPMT deficiency causes severe myelosuppression, and allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase and raises thiopurine toxicity, requiring a major dose reduction. Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, and in rheumatoid arthritis it is the anchor disease-modifying drug at low weekly dosing. Hazards are marrow suppression, hepatic fibrosis, pneumonitis, mucositis and teratogenicity; folic acid reduces some toxicities, and leucovorin rescues in high-dose overdose. Weekly rather than daily administration is a recognized safety issue. Cyclophosphamide, an alkylating agent used in vasculitis and lupus nephritis, causes hemorrhagic cystitis from acrolein, prevented with hydration and mesna.

Biologics target specific cytokines or cells. TNF-alpha inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept, certolizumab, golimumab) treat rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, psoriasis and spondyloarthropathy. They impair granuloma maintenance, so latent tuberculosis can reactivate, and patients are screened for tuberculosis and hepatitis B before therapy; they are also associated with demyelination, drug-induced lupus and worsened advanced heart failure. Infliximab is a chimeric antibody and can cause infusion reactions and anti-drug antibodies. Rituximab depletes CD20-positive B cells, used in lymphoma and autoimmune disease, with hepatitis B reactivation and rarely progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. Tocilizumab blocks the interleukin-6 receptor and can raise lipids and transaminases and cause gastrointestinal perforation. Abatacept blocks T-cell costimulation. Basiliximab blocks the IL-2 receptor in transplant induction.

Janus kinase inhibitors such as tofacitinib block cytokine signaling inside the cell. In ORAL Surveillance, in patients with cardiovascular risk factors, tofacitinib showed higher rates of major cardiovascular events, malignancy and thrombosis than TNF inhibitors, leading to boxed warnings; they also raise zoster risk.

Worked example: a patient with rheumatoid arthritis starting adalimumab has a positive interferon-gamma release assay. Latent tuberculosis should be treated first, because TNF blockade could allow reactivation.

lessons.title: Cell Wall Antibiotics: Beta-Lactams and Glycopeptides
body: Bacterial cells are protected by peptidoglycan, a mesh of sugar chains cross-linked by short peptides, and humans have no equivalent, which makes the wall an excellent selective target. Beta-lactam antibiotics mimic the D-alanyl-D-alanine terminus of the peptide chain and bind covalently to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), the transpeptidases that make the cross-links. The result is a weakened wall, autolysin activation and lysis of growing cells, so beta-lactams are time-dependent and bactericidal against actively dividing organisms.

Penicillins vary in spectrum. Penicillin G and V cover streptococci, many oral anaerobes and Treponema pallidum. Aminopenicillins (ampicillin, amoxicillin) add coverage of some gram-negative organisms and Enterococcus faecalis, but are hydrolyzed by beta-lactamases, so clavulanate, an inhibitor, is added. Antistaphylococcal penicillins (nafcillin, oxacillin, dicloxacillin) resist staphylococcal penicillinase. Antipseudomonal penicillins such as piperacillin, combined with tazobactam, cover many gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes. Cephalosporins are grouped in generations: first-generation agents (cefazolin) are strongest against gram-positive cocci and used for surgical prophylaxis; second-generation agents add some gram-negative and anaerobic activity; third-generation agents (ceftriaxone, cefotaxime) are strong against gram-negative bacilli and cross the blood-brain barrier for meningitis, with ceftazidime covering Pseudomonas; fourth-generation cefepime has broad antipseudomonal and gram-positive activity; and ceftaroline covers methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Cephalosporins do not cover enterococci or Listeria. Carbapenems (meropenem, imipenem, ertapenem) have the broadest spectrum and resist most beta-lactamases, but not carbapenemases. Imipenem is given with cilastatin to block renal dehydropeptidase and can lower the seizure threshold. Aztreonam, a
monobactam, covers only aerobic gram-negative rods, is safe in most penicillin-allergic patients and shares a side chain with ceftazidime.

Toxicities are mostly hypersensitivity: rash, urticaria, anaphylaxis, and rarely interstitial nephritis, hemolytic anemia and serum sickness. Cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is low and depends mainly on shared side chains, not the beta-lactam ring itself. Other effects include Clostridioides difficile infection from disrupting normal flora, ceftriaxone biliary sludge and its avoidance in neonates with hyperbilirubinemia and with calcium-containing intravenous solutions, and the prothrombin-time effects of agents with a methylthiotetrazole side chain such as cefotetan. Penicillin is renally cleared by tubular secretion, so probenecid prolongs its action.

Vancomycin is a glycopeptide, structurally different: it binds the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of the peptidoglycan precursor itself, blocking transglycosylation and transpeptidation. It is active only against gram-positive organisms and is used intravenously for MRSA and orally only for C. difficile because it is not absorbed. Infusion reaction (vancomycin infusion reaction, formerly red man syndrome) is a histamine-release flush slowed by infusing more slowly; other toxicities are nephrotoxicity and, rarely, ototoxicity, and dosing is guided by exposure monitoring. Resistance in enterococci arises when D-Ala-D-Ala is replaced by D-Ala-D-lactate, lowering binding affinity. Daptomycin, a lipopeptide, depolarizes the membrane of gram-positive organisms and is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant, so it is not used for pneumonia; it can cause myopathy.

Worked example: a patient with a history of an itchy rash after amoxicillin needs surgical prophylaxis. Because the cross-reactivity with cefazolin depends on its distinct side chain, cefazolin is generally acceptable after a non-severe, remote reaction, and allergy assessment is useful.

lessons.title: Protein Synthesis, DNA-Targeting and Folate Antibacterials
body: Bacterial ribosomes are 70S, built from 30S and 50S subunits, which differ from eukaryotic 80S ribosomes and give a selective target. Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) bind the 30S subunit, cause misreading of mRNA and block initiation, and are uniquely bactericidal among ribosomal drugs. Their uptake requires oxygen-dependent transport, so they do not work against anaerobes. They show concentration-dependent killing with a postantibiotic effect, which supports once-daily dosing. Toxicities are nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity (cochlear and vestibular, partly irreversible) and neuromuscular blockade, and the risk rises with loop diuretics, vancomycin and prolonged use. Streptomycin is a classic aminoglycoside used in tuberculosis.

Tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline) block the 30S A site, preventing tRNA binding; they are bacteriostatic and chelate divalent cations, so dairy and iron reduce absorption. They cover rickettsiae, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Borrelia and many atypical organisms, and are avoided in pregnancy, and the older tetracyclines in children under eight, because they deposit in bone and teeth, causing staining and growth effects. Doxycycline is the exception: CDC and AAP advise it at any age for suspected rickettsial disease such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever, because short courses have not been shown to stain permanent teeth. They also cause photosensitivity and esophagitis. Macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin) bind the 50S subunit and block translocation; they treat atypical pneumonia pathogens, are bacteriostatic, and share GI upset and QT prolongation. Erythromycin and clarithromycin inhibit CYP3A4, creating major interactions with statins, colchicine, calcineurin inhibitors and warfarin; azithromycin has far less CYP effect. Clindamycin binds 50S, covers anaerobes and gram-positive cocci, and carries a notable risk of C. difficile infection. Linezolid is an oxazolidinone that blocks initiation complex formation at 50S, treats VRE and MRSA, causes myelosuppression with prolonged use and, because it weakly inhibits monoamine oxidase, can contribute to serotonin
syndrome with serotonergic drugs. Chloramphenicol causes dose-related marrow suppression, rare aplastic anemia and gray baby syndrome from immature glucuronidation.

Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) inhibit DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) in gram-negative organisms and topoisomerase IV in gram-positive organisms, giving concentration-dependent bactericidal action. They are active against many gram-negative infections and, with levofloxacin and moxifloxacin, respiratory pathogens. Boxed warnings include tendinopathy and rupture (greater with corticosteroids and in older adults), peripheral neuropathy, central nervous system effects and myasthenia gravis exacerbation; others are QT prolongation, cartilage concerns in children, dysglycemia and aortic aneurysm risk. They chelate cations and ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2, raising theophylline and tizanidine levels.

Metronidazole forms reactive radicals in anaerobic organisms and protozoa that damage DNA; it covers anaerobes, Giardia, Trichomonas and C. difficile, and causes metallic taste, neuropathy and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole blocks two sequential steps of folate synthesis: sulfamethoxazole competes with PABA at dihydropteroate synthase, and trimethoprim inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase. It treats urinary infections and Pneumocystis, and its toxicities are rash and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, hyperkalemia (trimethoprim blocks ENaC), creatinine rise, marrow suppression with folate deficiency and kernicterus risk in the newborn. Nitrofurantoin concentrates in urine for uncomplicated cystitis and is avoided with impaired renal function.

Rifampin inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and is a potent inducer of CYP enzymes, which lowers levels of warfarin, oral contraceptives, tacrolimus, many antiretrovirals and others, and colors body fluids orange. Isoniazid inhibits mycolic acid synthesis, is activated by KatG, causes hepatitis and, by depleting pyridoxine, peripheral neuropathy, so vitamin B6 is co-administered. Pyrazinamide causes hyperuricemia, ethambutol optic neuritis and red-green color loss, and tuberculosis therapy uses combinations to prevent resistance.

Worked example: a young woman taking an oral contraceptive starts rifampin for tuberculosis. Enzyme induction accelerates estrogen metabolism, so contraceptive failure is a risk and another method is advised.

lessons.title: Antiviral Drugs and HIV Therapy
body: Viruses use host machinery, so antivirals target viral-specific enzymes or steps: entry, uncoating, nucleic acid polymerization, integration, protease processing and release. Many are nucleoside or nucleotide analogs that must be phosphorylated and then terminate chain elongation or inhibit the viral polymerase.

Herpesvirus agents illustrate selectivity. Acyclovir is a guanosine analog activated first by viral thymidine kinase, so it is concentrated in infected cells, then by host kinases; the triphosphate terminates viral DNA synthesis. It treats herpes simplex and varicella zoster infections, and its toxicity is crystal nephropathy if infused rapidly without hydration. Valacyclovir is a prodrug with better bioavailability. Ganciclovir is activated by the cytomegalovirus UL97 kinase and causes marrow suppression, especially neutropenia, and is teratogenic; valganciclovir is its oral prodrug. Foscarnet directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase without phosphorylation, so it works against thymidine-kinase-deficient acyclovir-resistant strains, and causes nephrotoxicity and electrolyte disturbances such as hypocalcemia. Cidofovir is nephrotoxic and given with probenecid. Influenza therapy includes the neuraminidase inhibitors oseltamivir and zanamivir, which block release of virions and work best when started early, and baloxavir, which inhibits cap-dependent endonuclease. Hepatitis C is now cured in most patients with direct-acting combinations that inhibit NS3/4A protease, NS5A, and NS5B polymerase (sofosbuvir is an NS5B nucleotide inhibitor); hepatitis B reactivation during treatment of hepatitis C in coinfected patients is a recognized hazard. Remdesivir is a nucleotide analog that
inhibits RNA-dependent RNA polymerase; nirmatrelvir inhibits the SARS-CoV-2 main protease and is given with ritonavir.

HIV therapy is combination antiretroviral therapy with at least two and usually three active drugs to suppress replication and avoid resistance. Major classes: nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs: tenofovir, emtricitabine, lamivudine, abacavir, zidovudine) act as chain terminators lacking a 3-prime hydroxyl. Abacavir hypersensitivity is associated with HLA-B*57:01 and requires screening before use. Tenofovir disoproxil is associated with renal tubular injury and bone loss, and the alafenamide form less so; zidovudine causes anemia; older agents cause lactic acidosis and lipoatrophy, and lamivudine, emtricitabine and tenofovir also treat hepatitis B, so stopping them in coinfected patients can cause a flare. Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (efavirenz, rilpivirine, doravirine) bind an allosteric site; efavirenz causes vivid dreams and neuropsychiatric effects. Integrase strand transfer inhibitors (dolutegravir, bictegravir, raltegravir) block insertion of viral DNA into host chromosomes; they are generally well tolerated, favored in first-line regimens in current guidelines, and chelate polyvalent cations, so antacids and iron are separated. Protease inhibitors (darunavir, atazanavir) block cleavage of viral polyproteins and are often pharmacologically boosted by ritonavir or cobicistat. Those boosters inhibit CYP3A4, creating large interactions

with statins such as simvastatin, certain steroids, sedatives and many others. Entry inhibitors include maraviroc, which blocks CCR5 and requires a tropism test, and fusion inhibitors. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome can occur when therapy restores immunity and unmasks an opportunistic infection.

Worked example: a patient starting a ritonavir-boosted regimen takes simvastatin and develops rhabdomyolysis. CYP3A4 inhibition by ritonavir raised statin levels, so the statin should be switched to one not dependent on CYP3A4 such as rosuvastatin or pravastatin, with appropriate dosing.

lessons.title: Antifungal Drugs
body: Fungi are eukaryotes, so selectivity depends on differences in the cell membrane and wall. The fungal membrane contains ergosterol rather than cholesterol, and the wall contains beta-1,3-glucan, which humans lack. Each class exploits one of these features.

Amphotericin B is a polyene that binds ergosterol and forms pores, causing leakage and death, so it is fungicidal against a broad range of yeasts and molds. It also binds human cholesterol to a lesser degree, which explains toxicities: infusion-related fever, chills and rigors (reduced by premedication and slower infusion), nephrotoxicity from afferent vasoconstriction and tubular injury with hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia and renal tubular acidosis, and anemia. Liposomal formulations are less nephrotoxic and, with flucytosine, form the induction regimen for cryptococcal meningitis. Nystatin is a topical polyene used for mucosal candidiasis. Flucytosine is converted by fungal cytosine deaminase into 5-fluorouracil, inhibiting DNA and RNA synthesis, causes marrow suppression, and is used in combination because resistance emerges quickly.

Azoles inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, a cytochrome P450 enzyme, blocking ergosterol synthesis and giving a fungistatic effect against yeasts. Because they inhibit human CYP enzymes to varying degrees, drug interactions are central. Fluconazole penetrates the central nervous system and treats candidiasis and cryptococcal disease; it is teratogenic with high doses, prolongs QT and inhibits CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 moderately. Itraconazole needs gastric acid for oral absorption and is negatively inotropic, so it is avoided in heart failure. Voriconazole is first-line for invasive aspergillosis and causes transient visual disturbances, hallucinations and hepatotoxicity, with variable CYP2C19 metabolism. Posaconazole and isavuconazole extend coverage to Mucorales. Ketoconazole inhibits steroidogenesis, causing gynecomastia and adrenal suppression, and serious hepatotoxicity has limited systemic use. Many azoles are strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, and so interact with statins, calcineurin inhibitors, warfarin and QT-prolonging drugs.

Echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) inhibit beta-1,3-glucan synthase, weakening the wall. They are fungicidal against Candida, fungistatic against Aspergillus, are first-line for invasive candidiasis, have few interactions, and cause infusion reactions and mild hepatic enzyme elevations; they lack activity against Cryptococcus. Terbinafine inhibits squalene epoxidase, causing toxic squalene accumulation and ergosterol depletion; it is used in dermatophyte and nail infections, with hepatotoxicity and taste disturbance. Griseofulvin disrupts microtubules in dermatophytes. Both topical and oral therapy for onychomycosis are monitored for hepatic effects.

Resistance to azoles occurs through efflux pumps, target gene mutation and overexpression, and Candida glabrata and Candida auris are of particular concern for reduced susceptibility, with C. auris often multidrug resistant. Echinocandin resistance arises from FKS mutations.

Worked example: a patient with HIV and cryptococcal meningitis receives liposomal amphotericin B with flucytosine for induction and then fluconazole for consolidation. Monitoring includes renal function, potassium and magnesium for amphotericin and blood counts for flucytosine.

lessons.title: Antimicrobial Resistance and Stewardship
body: Antibiotic use exerts selective pressure. In any large bacterial population a few cells carry a resistance trait through mutation or acquired genes; the drug eliminates susceptible competitors and leaves resistant ones to expand. Resistance genes spread horizontally by conjugation of plasmids, transformation and transduction by bacteriophage, so resistance can cross species. Understanding mechanisms predicts which drugs fail and why.

Four mechanisms recur. Drug inactivation: beta-lactamases hydrolyze the beta-lactam ring, with extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs) hydrolyzing penicillins, cephalosporins and aztreonam but not carbapenems, which are therefore the usual choice for serious ESBL infections. AmpC enzymes confer resistance to many cephalosporins and are induced during therapy in organisms such as Enterobacter, which is why cefepime or carbapenems are often preferred. Carbapenemases (KPC, NDM, OXA-48 and others) hydrolyze carbapenems, and newer beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations such as ceftazidime-avibactam cover some of them. Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes act similarly. Target alteration: methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus carries mecA, encoding PBP2a, a low-affinity penicillin-binding protein, so all beta-lactams except those specifically designed to bind it, such as ceftaroline, fail; vancomycin-resistant enterococci substitute D-Ala-D-lactate; fluoroquinolone resistance arises from gyrA and parC mutations; and macrolide resistance involves ribosomal methylation by erm genes, which also causes inducible clindamycin resistance. Reduced access and efflux: porin loss in gram-negative bacteria reduces carbapenem entry, and efflux pumps expel tetracyclines, macrolides and fluoroquinolones. Bypass pathways: bacteria acquire alternative folate enzymes insensitive to trimethoprim or sulfonamides.

Pharmacodynamics guide dosing logic. Beta-lactams and vancomycin kill best when drug concentrations stay above the minimum inhibitory concentration for a large fraction of the dosing interval (time-dependent killing), so frequent or extended dosing is rational. Aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones show concentration-dependent killing, where the peak relative to the MIC (or the area under the curve over MIC for fluoroquinolones) predicts efficacy, so they use high, less frequent dosing. A postantibiotic effect extends suppression after levels fall.

Stewardship programs aim to give the right drug, for the right duration, with the narrowest effective spectrum. Core practices: obtain cultures before antibiotics where possible, start broad empiric therapy for serious infection but narrow when susceptibilities return (de-escalation), switch from intravenous to oral therapy when appropriate, use the shortest course supported by evidence, avoid treating colonization such as asymptomatic bacteriuria in most patients, and clarify penicillin allergy labels, since most patients labeled allergic tolerate penicillins. Antibiotics also drive Clostridioides difficile, and first-line treatment is oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin, with metronidazole reserved for specific situations; fecal microbiota products are used for recurrence. Infection control, vaccination and diagnostics complement stewardship. Combination therapy is used for tuberculosis and HIV to prevent resistance, and sometimes for synergy (a cell-wall agent plus an aminoglycoside in enterococcal endocarditis).

Worked example: a patient with an Enterobacter bloodstream infection improves on ceftriaxone, then relapses with resistance. Inducible chromosomal AmpC enzyme production was selected under cephalosporin pressure, so cefepime or a carbapenem would have been a better initial choice.

lessons.title: Antidepressants and Serotonin Syndrome
body: Most antidepressants raise synaptic monoamine signaling by blocking reuptake transporters or monoamine oxidase, though clinical benefit takes several weeks, which implies downstream adaptation rather than a simple rise in transmitter. Selection among agents is largely driven by side-effect profile, comorbidity and interactions, since efficacy across classes is broadly similar, as the large STAR*D effectiveness study illustrated with its stepwise approach.

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (sertraline, fluoxetine, escitalopram, citalopram, paroxetine) block the serotonin transporter and are first-line for depression, anxiety disorders and obsessive-compulsive disorder. Common effects are nausea and diarrhea early, sexual dysfunction, insomnia or somnolence, and weight change. They can cause hyponatremia through SIADH, particularly in older adults, and increase bleeding risk because platelets store serotonin, which matters with NSAIDs and anticoagulants. Citalopram has a dose-related QT effect. Paroxetine is the most anticholinergic and has the strongest discontinuation syndrome with short half-life, while fluoxetine has a very long half-life, so it self-tapers, and it inhibits CYP2D6, raising levels of metoprolol, tricyclics and tamoxifen activation is reduced. All antidepressants carry a boxed warning for increased suicidal thinking in children, adolescents and young adults, which calls for monitoring at initiation. Venlafaxine and duloxetine (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) add noradrenergic effects, with dose-related blood pressure elevation for venlafaxine and benefit in neuropathic pain for duloxetine.

Tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine) block serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake but also muscarinic, histamine H1 and alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, and cardiac sodium channels. This gives anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, confusion), sedation, orthostatic hypotension and weight gain. In overdose, sodium channel blockade widens the QRS complex and causes arrhythmias, seizures and hypotension, and treatment includes intravenous sodium bicarbonate, which narrows the QRS by raising extracellular sodium and alkalinizing. Because of the narrow safety margin, they are used with caution in patients at risk of self-harm.

Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (phenelzine, tranylcypromine, selegiline patch) irreversibly inhibit MAO. Dietary tyramine, normally degraded by gut MAO-A, then enters the circulation and displaces norepinephrine from nerve terminals, causing a hypertensive crisis after aged cheeses and cured meats. Combining an MAOI with serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, meperidine, dextromethorphan, linezolid, tramadol) or sympathomimetics risks serotonin syndrome or hypertensive crisis. A washout of about two weeks separates an MAOI from other antidepressants, and about five weeks after fluoxetine because of its long active metabolite.

Atypical agents add flexibility. Bupropion inhibits norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake, lacks sexual dysfunction, assists smoking cessation, and lowers the seizure threshold, so it is contraindicated in seizure disorders, eating disorders and abrupt alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal. Mirtazapine blocks alpha-2 autoreceptors plus 5-HT2 and H1 receptors, causing sedation and weight gain, which can help in insomnia and cachexia. Trazodone is sedating and can cause priapism. Ketamine and its enantiomer esketamine, NMDA receptor antagonists, offer rapid effect in treatment-resistant depression with dissociation and blood pressure rise.

Serotonin syndrome is excess serotonergic stimulation, presenting with agitation, hyperthermia, diaphoresis, diarrhea, tremor, hyperreflexia and inducible or ocular clonus, usually within hours of a new drug or dose. It differs from neuroleptic malignant syndrome by rapid onset, hyperreflexia and clonus rather than lead-pipe rigidity with bradyreflexia. Treatment is to stop the agents, give benzodiazepines and supportive cooling, with cyproheptadine, a 5-HT2A antagonist, if needed.

Worked example: a patient on an SSRI is given tramadol after surgery and develops sweating, tremor and clonus with a temperature of 39 degrees. This is serotonin syndrome from additive serotonergic activity, not infection.

lessons.title: Antipsychotics and Lithium
body: Antipsychotics reduce positive psychotic symptoms mainly by blocking dopamine D2 receptors in the mesolimbic pathway. The same blockade in other pathways produces the main adverse effects: in the nigrostriatal pathway, extrapyramidal symptoms; in the tuberoinfundibular pathway, hyperprolactinemia because dopamine normally inhibits prolactin; and in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, antiemetic effect. Receptors for histamine, muscarinic acetylcholine and alpha-1 adrenergic ligands add sedation and weight gain, anticholinergic effects and orthostasis.

First-generation agents (haloperidol, chlorpromazine, fluphenazine) are potent D2 blockers. High-potency agents like haloperidol cause more extrapyramidal effects; low-potency agents like chlorpromazine cause more sedation, anticholinergic effects and hypotension. Thioridazine causes QT prolongation and retinal deposits, and chlorpromazine causes corneal and skin pigment changes. The extrapyramidal syndromes have a timeline worth memorizing: acute dystonia occurs within hours to days and responds to anticholinergics such as benztropine or diphenhydramine; akathisia, a subjective restlessness, appears within days to weeks and is treated by lowering the dose, adding a beta blocker like propranolol or a benzodiazepine; parkinsonism appears over days to weeks and responds to anticholinergics; tardive dyskinesia, involuntary orofacial and limb movements, arises after months to years and is treated with VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) and by switching to a lower-risk agent. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a rare emergency of fever, severe lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, altered mental status and raised creatine kinase, treated by stopping the drug, cooling, benzodiazepines, and dantrolene or bromocriptine in severe cases.

Second-generation agents block serotonin 5-HT2A receptors as well as D2 and generally cause fewer extrapyramidal effects, but carry metabolic risk (weight gain, dyslipidemia, diabetes), greatest for olanzapine and clozapine. Risperidone and paliperidone produce notable hyperprolactinemia. Quetiapine is sedating. Ziprasidone prolongs QT. Aripiprazole and brexpiprazole are D2 partial agonists, with akathisia as a typical effect. The CATIE trial found that second-generation agents had no striking efficacy advantage over perphenazine for most outcomes in chronic schizophrenia, and high discontinuation rates for all. All antipsychotics carry a boxed warning for increased mortality in older adults with dementia-related psychosis.

Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and reduces suicidality. It is unique because of severe neutropenia and agranulocytosis, requiring regular absolute neutrophil count monitoring. The FDA removed the clozapine REMS program in 2025, but the boxed warning and the neutrophil monitoring schedule in the label remain; other risks are seizures, myocarditis early in therapy, orthostatic hypotension, sialorrhea and constipation that can progress to bowel obstruction, and metabolic effects. It is metabolized by CYP1A2, so smoking cessation raises levels and ciprofloxacin or fluvoxamine can cause toxicity.

Lithium is a mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder with a narrow therapeutic window. It is eliminated entirely by the kidney, handled like sodium in the proximal tubule, so sodium depletion, thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and NSAIDs raise lithium levels. Chronic toxicities include tremor, hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from reduced collecting duct response to ADH, weight gain and, in pregnancy, a risk of fetal cardiac malformation (Ebstein anomaly). Acute toxicity causes coarse tremor, vomiting, ataxia, confusion and seizures, and hemodialysis is used in severe poisoning. Valproate, carbamazepine and lamotrigine are alternative mood stabilizers.

Worked example: a young man given haloperidol develops sustained neck and eye deviation with painful muscle spasm two hours later. This is acute dystonia, and an intramuscular anticholinergic gives rapid relief.

lessons.title: Sedative-Hypnotics and Anxiolytics
body: The main inhibitory neurotransmitter of the brain is GABA, acting at the GABA-A receptor, a pentameric chloride channel. Several sedative-hypnotics enhance its action at distinct sites, and the differences explain their safety. Benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, alprazolam, clonazepam, midazolam) bind between alpha and gamma subunits and increase the frequency of channel opening in the presence of GABA. Because they require endogenous GABA, they have a ceiling to their effect and a wide margin of safety when used alone. Barbiturates (phenobarbital, thiopental) bind a different site and increase the duration of channel opening, and at higher concentrations open the channel directly, so effect has no ceiling and overdose can cause fatal respiratory depression. Nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics (zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone) act on the benzodiazepine site with selectivity for alpha-1 containing receptors, and can cause complex sleep behaviors such as sleepwalking and driving.

Benzodiazepines are used for anxiety, panic, insomnia, seizures and status epilepticus, alcohol withdrawal, muscle spasm, procedural sedation and as premedication. Adverse effects include sedation, anterograde amnesia, impaired psychomotor function and falls in the elderly, tolerance and dependence, and rebound or withdrawal syndromes on abrupt discontinuation that can include seizures, so they are tapered. Respiratory depression is modest alone but substantial when combined with opioids or alcohol, which led to a boxed warning on opioid-benzodiazepine co-use, and later class boxed warnings on abuse, misuse and dependence. Pharmacokinetics decide the clinical choice: diazepam and chlordiazepoxide have long-acting active metabolites that accumulate in the elderly and in liver disease. Lorazepam, oxazepam and temazepam are cleared by direct glucuronidation, bypassing the oxidative phase I step, so they are preferred in the elderly and in hepatic impairment. Midazolam is short-acting and used for sedation. Flumazenil is a competitive benzodiazepine-site antagonist that reverses benzodiazepine sedation, but may precipitate seizures in dependent patients or those who co-ingested pro-convulsant drugs such as tricyclics.

Buspirone is a partial agonist at 5-HT1A receptors, used for generalized anxiety. It is minimally sedating, has no abuse potential and no muscle relaxant or anticonvulsant action, and needs weeks to work, so it is unsuitable for acute panic. Ramelteon is a melatonin MT1 and MT2 agonist for sleep onset. Suvorexant and similar drugs block orexin receptors. Hydroxyzine is a sedating H1 antihistamine with anxiolytic effect. Propranolol blunts peripheral autonomic symptoms of performance anxiety. Antidepressants such as SSRIs are first-line for long-term treatment of most anxiety disorders, with benzodiazepines used as short-term bridges.

Alcohol withdrawal is clinically important: chronic ethanol exposure downregulates GABA-A and upregulates NMDA signaling, so abrupt abstinence causes tremor, hyperadrenergic features, seizures within roughly the first one to two days and delirium tremens later. Benzodiazepines are first-line treatment, and thiamine is given to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.

Worked example: an older woman on a long-acting benzodiazepine for sleep falls and fractures her hip. Accumulation of active metabolites and impaired psychomotor function contributed, and a taper rather than abrupt cessation is needed.

lessons.title: Antiepileptic Drugs
body: Seizures result from excessive synchronous neuronal firing, and antiepileptic drugs reduce excitability by one of a few mechanisms: blocking voltage-gated sodium channels in a use-dependent way, enhancing GABA-mediated inhibition, blocking T-type calcium channels, or modulating synaptic vesicle release. Agents are matched to seizure type, and many have major interactions and teratogenic risks.

Phenytoin and fosphenytoin block sodium channels. Phenytoin follows saturable (zero-order) metabolism at therapeutic levels, so a small dose increase can cause a disproportionate rise in concentration with nystagmus, ataxia and confusion. Chronic toxicity includes gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, peripheral neuropathy, osteomalacia from vitamin D metabolism and megaloblastic anemia, and it induces CYP enzymes. Intravenous phenytoin can cause cardiac arrhythmias and hypotension and tissue injury, so fosphenytoin is preferred. Fetal hydantoin syndrome is a teratogenic effect. Carbamazepine also blocks sodium channels and is first-line for focal seizures and trigeminal neuralgia. Its toxicities are hyponatremia (SIADH), bone marrow suppression including aplastic anemia and agranulocytosis, hepatotoxicity, diplopia and ataxia; Stevens-Johnson syndrome is associated with HLA-B*15:02 in people of Asian ancestry, which requires screening. It is a strong CYP3A4 inducer, including induction of its own metabolism, and so lowers levels of oral contraceptives, warfarin and many other drugs.
