Valproate raises GABA and blocks sodium and T-type calcium channels, and is the broad-spectrum choice for generalized epilepsies, including absence and myoclonic seizures. Its toxicities are hepatotoxicity (greater in young children with metabolic disease), pancreatitis, hyperammonemia, tremor, weight gain and thrombocytopenia, and it is a major teratogen causing neural tube defects and lower cognitive outcomes, so it is avoided in people who may become pregnant when alternatives exist. It inhibits metabolism of lamotrigine. Lamotrigine blocks sodium channels, is broad-spectrum and well tolerated, but life-threatening rash, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, is minimized by very slow titration, and doses must be halved when combined with valproate. Estrogen-containing contraceptives reduce lamotrigine levels. Ethosuximide blocks thalamic T-type calcium channels and is first-line for absence epilepsy without other seizure types, with nausea and headache.

Levetiracetam binds synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, has few interactions, and causes irritability, mood changes and somnolence. Topiramate blocks sodium channels, enhances GABA and weakly inhibits carbonic anhydrase, so it causes metabolic acidosis, kidney stones, paresthesia, word-finding difficulty, weight loss and angle-closure glaucoma, and carries a risk of oral clefts. Gabapentin and pregabalin bind the alpha-2-delta subunit of calcium channels, useful for focal seizures and neuropathic pain with sedation and dizziness. Phenobarbital enhances GABA-A duration of opening and is inexpensive with broad CYP induction. Benzodiazepines act rapidly on status epilepticus.

Status epilepticus is an emergency treated first with a benzodiazepine (intravenous lorazepam, or intramuscular midazolam if no access), followed by a second-line antiseizure drug such as fosphenytoin, valproate or levetiracetam; ESETT found these three similarly effective for benzodiazepine-refractory status. Enzyme-inducing drugs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) reduce the effect of oral contraceptives and increase vitamin D and folate needs. Antiepileptics carry a class warning for suicidal ideation and are tapered rather than stopped abruptly.
Worked example: a child with absence seizures only is best treated with ethosuximide because it targets T-type thalamic channels, whereas carbamazepine can worsen absence seizures.

lessons.title: Anesthetics and Neuromuscular Blockers
body: General anesthesia produces unconsciousness, amnesia, immobility and analgesia, usually through balanced combinations. Inhaled agents (sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, nitrous oxide) are characterized by two properties. Minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) is the concentration preventing movement in 50 percent of patients at incision, and inversely reflects potency. The blood:gas partition coefficient reflects solubility: a poorly soluble agent (desflurane, nitrous oxide) equilibrates quickly between alveoli and brain, giving fast induction and emergence, while a more soluble agent (halothane, isoflurane) acts more slowly. Volatile agents cause dose-dependent vasodilation, hypotension and respiratory depression. Nitrous oxide causes diffusion hypoxia at emergence, expands closed air spaces, and irreversibly oxidizes vitamin B12, impairing methionine synthase. Halothane can cause immune-mediated hepatitis. Sevoflurane is a favored induction agent, with a degradation product, compound A, of theoretical renal concern at low flows.

Malignant hyperthermia is a pharmacogenetic emergency, usually due to ryanodine receptor (RYR1) variants, triggered by volatile agents and succinylcholine. Uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum causes hypermetabolism, with rising end-tidal carbon dioxide, rigidity, hyperthermia, tachycardia, acidosis, hyperkalemia and rhabdomyolysis. Dantrolene, which blocks the ryanodine receptor, is the antidote, and triggers are stopped.

Intravenous induction agents differ. Propofol enhances GABA-A function, gives rapid smooth induction and antiemetic effect, and causes hypotension and apnea; prolonged high-dose infusion can cause propofol infusion syndrome, and the lipid vehicle can support bacterial growth. Etomidate also acts on GABA-A, preserves hemodynamic stability but inhibits adrenal 11-beta-hydroxylase and so briefly suppresses cortisol, and can cause myoclonus and nausea. Ketamine antagonizes the NMDA receptor to produce dissociative anesthesia, with increased heart rate and blood pressure through catecholamine release, bronchodilation and emergence reactions with hallucinations; it is useful in hypotensive and asthmatic patients, with caution in raised intracranial pressure and coronary disease. Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2 agonist for sedation without respiratory depression, with bradycardia and hypotension. Benzodiazepines such as midazolam provide anxiolysis and amnesia.

Local anesthetics block voltage-gated sodium channels from inside the neuron, in their open or inactivated state, so smaller, more rapidly firing fibers are blocked first, and pain and temperature fibers are blocked before pressure and motor. Amides (lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine; names contain two i) are hepatically metabolized, while esters (procaine, tetracaine, chloroprocaine) are broken down by plasma cholinesterase and produce the PABA metabolite that can cause allergy. Infected tissue is acidic, which raises the ionized fraction and reduces tissue penetration. Epinephrine causes vasoconstriction, prolonging the block and reducing systemic absorption. Systemic toxicity begins with perioral numbness, tinnitus and metallic taste, then seizures, followed by arrhythmias and cardiovascular collapse; bupivacaine is especially cardiotoxic, and intravenous lipid emulsion rescues local anesthetic toxicity.

Neuromuscular blockers allow intubation and relaxation. Succinylcholine is a depolarizing agent: it persistently activates nicotinic receptors, producing initial fasciculations then paralysis, and is hydrolyzed by plasma cholinesterase, so deficiency prolongs block. It can cause hyperkalemia in burns, crush injuries, denervation and prolonged immobility because of upregulated receptors, and is a malignant hyperthermia trigger. Nondepolarizing agents (rocuronium, vecuronium, cisatracurium) competitively antagonize the receptor. Cisatracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination, independent of organ function. Reversal uses acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as neostigmine, given with an antimuscarinic like glycopyrrolate to prevent bradycardia, or sugammadex, which encapsulates rocuronium and vecuronium.

Worked example: a child with hyperthermia, rigidity and rising end-tidal carbon dioxide soon after induction with sevoflurane and succinylcholine has malignant hyperthermia, and dantrolene is the specific treatment.

lessons.title: Opioids and Their Antagonists
body: Opioids act on G-protein-coupled receptors (mu, kappa and delta) in the brain, spinal cord and gut. The mu receptor mediates most analgesia and its toxicities. Through Gi/o signaling, it lowers cyclic AMP, opens potassium channels and closes presynaptic calcium channels, so neurons hyperpolarize and release less transmitter. Clinical effects are analgesia, euphoria, sedation, respiratory depression through reduced brainstem sensitivity to carbon dioxide, cough suppression, nausea through the chemoreceptor trigger zone, and miosis through the oculomotor nucleus, together with reduced gut motility and increased smooth muscle tone.

The overdose triad is depressed consciousness, respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils. Tolerance develops to analgesia, euphoria, sedation and respiratory depression, but little tolerance develops to miosis and constipation, so constipation is anticipated and treated with a stimulant or osmotic laxative alongside long-term use. Other effects include urinary retention, biliary spasm (sphincter of Oddi), histamine release causing flushing and itching, and hypotension, which is greater with morphine. Physical dependence produces a withdrawal syndrome of rhinorrhea, lacrimation, yawning, mydriasis, piloerection, diarrhea, abdominal cramping and myalgias, uncomfortable but not generally life-threatening, in contrast to alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal.

Individual agents have distinct features. Morphine is hydrophilic and metabolized to morphine-6-glucuronide, which is active and accumulates in renal failure. Fentanyl is highly lipophilic and potent, with rapid onset, and illicit fentanyl is the main driver of overdose deaths. Hydromorphone is a potent alternative in renal impairment. Oxycodone and hydrocodone are common oral agents. Codeine is a prodrug converted by CYP2D6 to morphine, so ultrarapid metabolizers risk toxicity and poor metabolizers get little analgesia; it is avoided in children after tonsillectomy and in breastfeeding. Meperidine produces a neurotoxic metabolite, normeperidine, which can cause seizures, and is serotonergic, so it is dangerous with monoamine oxidase inhibitors. Tramadol is a weak mu agonist and also inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake, with seizure and serotonin syndrome risk. Methadone, a long-acting full agonist and NMDA antagonist, treats pain and opioid use disorder; it prolongs QT, has a long and variable half-life that makes overdose risk highest during initiation, and interacts with CYP3A4 and CYP2B6 modulators.

Buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial agonist at the mu receptor, so it has a ceiling on respiratory depression and a better safety profile, and is used for opioid use disorder. Because it binds tightly but with limited activation, giving it to a patient with a full agonist on board can displace the full agonist and precipitate withdrawal. Naloxone is a competitive mu antagonist given intranasally or intravenously to reverse overdose; its duration of action is shorter than many opioids, particularly long-acting ones or fentanyl in large amounts, so renarcotization can occur and monitoring or repeat dosing is necessary. In a dependent patient, it precipitates withdrawal. Naltrexone is a long-acting oral or monthly injectable antagonist used for opioid use disorder after detoxification and for alcohol use disorder, with hepatic monitoring and a risk of precipitated withdrawal if opioids remain. Methadone and buprenorphine reduce mortality in opioid use disorder, and the CDC 2022 guideline emphasizes individualized, cautious prescribing for pain with attention to nonopioid options and not abruptly tapering patients on long-term therapy.

Worked example: a man found unresponsive with pinpoint pupils and slow breathing improves after intranasal naloxone, then becomes drowsy again 40 minutes later. The antagonist wore off before the long-acting opioid did, so observation and repeat dosing are needed.

lessons.title: Cytotoxic Chemotherapy Principles
body: Cytotoxic drugs kill cells that are dividing, so rapidly renewing normal tissues are damaged alongside tumor: marrow, gut mucosa, hair follicles and gonads. This is why myelosuppression, mucositis, nausea and alopecia are shared toxicities, and why organ-specific toxicities define each drug class. The fractional kill hypothesis states that each cycle kills a constant fraction of tumor cells rather than a fixed number, so cure requires repeated cycles and combination regimens that use drugs with different mechanisms and non-overlapping toxicities to minimize resistance. Chemotherapy is given in cycles to allow normal marrow recovery.

Drugs are grouped by cell cycle effect. Cell-cycle-specific agents act in particular phases: antimetabolites (methotrexate, 5-fluorouracil, cytarabine, 6-mercaptopurine) in S phase, bleomycin in G2, and vinca alkaloids and taxanes in M phase. Alkylating agents and platinum compounds are cell-cycle nonspecific.

Alkylating agents add alkyl groups to DNA and cross-link strands. Cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide are prodrugs activated in the liver; their metabolite acrolein damages the bladder epithelium, causing hemorrhagic cystitis, which mesna binds and hydration reduces. Nitrosoureas cross the blood-brain barrier and cause delayed marrow suppression. Platinum agents also cross-link DNA: cisplatin causes nephrotoxicity (mitigated by hydration and amifostine), ototoxicity, peripheral neuropathy and severe emesis; carboplatin is more myelosuppressive and less nephrotoxic. Antimetabolites mimic substrates: methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (rescued with leucovorin), 5-fluorouracil inhibits thymidylate synthase and causes mucositis, diarrhea and hand-foot syndrome, with severe toxicity in patients deficient in dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase, and cytarabine causes cerebellar toxicity and myelosuppression. 6-Mercaptopurine is inactivated by TPMT and xanthine oxidase.

Anthracyclines (doxorubicin, daunorubicin) intercalate DNA, inhibit topoisomerase II and generate free radicals. The signature toxicity is cumulative, dose-dependent cardiomyopathy, which dexrazoxane, an iron chelator, can reduce; baseline and serial cardiac function monitoring is standard. Bleomycin causes dose-related pulmonary fibrosis, rare skin changes, and little marrow suppression, and is monitored with pulmonary function. Topoisomerase I inhibitors (irinotecan, topotecan) can cause diarrhea, and UGT1A1 variants reduce inactivation of the active metabolite of irinotecan. Etoposide inhibits topoisomerase II. Vinca alkaloids (vincristine, vinblastine) block microtubule assembly: vincristine causes peripheral neuropathy and constipation or ileus, with little marrow suppression, and is fatal if given intrathecally; vinblastine is more myelosuppressive. Taxanes (paclitaxel, docetaxel) stabilize microtubules and block disassembly, causing neuropathy, hypersensitivity reactions (hence premedication with a steroid and antihistamines), and neutropenia.

Supportive and rescue therapies form part of the pharmacology. Leucovorin rescues methotrexate. Mesna protects the bladder. Dexrazoxane limits anthracycline cardiotoxicity. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor shortens neutropenia. Antiemetic regimens combine 5-HT3 antagonists, NK1 antagonists and dexamethasone. Tumor lysis syndrome follows rapid killing of bulky, chemosensitive tumors such as high-grade lymphomas and leukemias, releasing potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids, which produces hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia and hyperuricemia with acute kidney injury; prevention uses hydration, allopurinol, or rasburicase, which converts uric acid to allantoin and is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency because of hemolysis and methemoglobinemia.

Worked example: a patient treated for a germ cell tumor with bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin develops hearing loss and rising creatinine after several cycles. These are cisplatin toxicities, which hydration and monitoring aim to limit, and later dyspnea or cough should prompt consideration of bleomycin lung injury.

lessons.title: Targeted, Hormonal and Immune Cancer Therapy
body: Targeted therapy aims at molecular drivers that tumors depend on, which gives a different toxicity profile from cytotoxics and requires biomarker selection, because efficacy is tied to a specific alteration. The classic proof of principle is imatinib, which inhibits the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase created by the Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myeloid leukemia; it also inhibits KIT, so it works in gastrointestinal stromal tumors. Resistance commonly arises from kinase domain mutations, prompting second- and third-generation inhibitors. Its toxicities include fluid retention, edema and myelosuppression. Epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitors (erlotinib, osimertinib) treat EGFR-mutant lung cancer with rash and diarrhea as typical effects, and BRAF inhibitors (vemurafenib, dabrafenib) treat BRAF V600E-mutant melanoma and are combined with MEK inhibitors to reduce resistance and the skin proliferative effects of paradoxical pathway activation.

Monoclonal antibodies exploit surface targets. Trastuzumab binds HER2 in HER2-positive breast and gastric cancers and can cause cardiomyopathy, which is reversible and not cumulative-dose related in the manner of anthracyclines, so it requires cardiac monitoring, particularly if combined with or following an anthracycline. Rituximab targets CD20 on B cells, causing infusion reactions and risk of hepatitis B reactivation. Bevacizumab neutralizes vascular endothelial growth factor, so it causes hypertension, proteinuria, bleeding, thromboembolism, gastrointestinal perforation and impaired wound healing. Cetuximab targets EGFR and is ineffective in tumors with RAS mutations. Antibody-drug conjugates combine an antibody with a cytotoxic payload to improve selectivity.

Endocrine therapy exploits hormone dependence. Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator, antagonizing the receptor in breast tissue while acting as an agonist in the endometrium and bone. This explains reduced breast cancer recurrence and preserved bone density, together with increased risk of endometrial cancer and thromboembolism and hot flashes. Its activation involves CYP2D6, so strong inhibitors such as fluoxetine and paroxetine can reduce efficacy. Aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole, letrozole) block estrogen synthesis in peripheral tissue and are used in postmenopausal women, causing arthralgia and bone loss. In premenopausal women ovarian suppression is needed first. In prostate cancer, GnRH agonists (leuprolide) first raise luteinizing hormone and cause a testosterone flare before suppression, so an antiandrogen is given first to blunt the flare; androgen receptor blockers (enzalutamide, bicalutamide) and abiraterone, a CYP17 inhibitor given with prednisone to prevent mineralocorticoid excess, extend therapy.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors release brakes on T cells. Antibodies against PD-1 (pembrolizumab, nivolumab), PD-L1 (atezolizumab) or CTLA-4 (ipilimumab) restore antitumor immunity and have transformed treatment of melanoma, lung cancer and many others, particularly in tumors with high mutational burden or microsatellite instability. Their toxicities are immune-related adverse events: colitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis, dermatitis, endocrinopathies such as thyroiditis, hypophysitis, adrenal insufficiency and diabetes, and rare myocarditis. These are managed by holding the drug and giving glucocorticoids, with permanent replacement for endocrine failure. Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy can cause cytokine release syndrome, treated with tocilizumab, and neurotoxicity.

Worked example: a patient on pembrolizumab develops several weeks later profuse diarrhea and abdominal pain. Immune-mediated colitis is likely, and the approach is to hold therapy, exclude infection and treat with glucocorticoids, adding other immunosuppression if refractory.

lessons.title: Toxicology: Mechanisms and Antidotes
body: Toxicology follows a consistent method: stabilize the airway, breathing and circulation; identify the toxidrome from the pattern of vital signs, pupils, skin and mental status; decontaminate or enhance elimination when this will help; and give a specific antidote when one exists. Many antidotes work by competing for a receptor, restoring a depleted cofactor, binding the toxin, or blocking formation of the toxic metabolite, so mechanism predicts the antidote.

Toxidromes are pattern recognition. Opioids give miosis, respiratory depression and coma. Sympathomimetics such as cocaine and amphetamines give agitation, mydriasis, tachycardia, hypertension and diaphoresis. Anticholinergics give mydriasis, dry skin, urinary retention, hyperthermia and delirium ("dry as a bone, red as a beet, mad as a hatter"). Cholinergic poisoning from organophosphates and carbamates gives salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, bronchorrhea, bradycardia, miosis and muscle fasciculations. Sedative-hypnotics give depressed consciousness with normal pupils and relatively normal vital signs. Serotonin syndrome gives clonus and hyperreflexia, and salicylate poisoning gives tinnitus, hyperventilation, fever and mixed acid-base disturbance.

Specific antidotes: Naloxone antagonizes opioids at the mu receptor, and flumazenil antagonizes benzodiazepines but can provoke seizures in dependent patients. N-acetylcysteine regenerates glutathione in acetaminophen poisoning. Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, so treatment is atropine, titrated to drying of bronchial secretions, plus pralidoxime, which reactivates the enzyme if given early before the inhibited enzyme "ages". Methanol and ethylene glycol are metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase to formic acid and to glycolate and oxalate, respectively; fomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing formation of toxic metabolites, and dialysis removes the toxins and acid in severe cases. Methanol causes visual disturbance and ethylene glycol causes calcium oxalate crystals, an anion-gap acidosis and renal failure. Cyanide blocks cytochrome oxidase and halts aerobic metabolism; hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide, with sodium nitrite and thiosulfate as alternatives. Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with high affinity and shifts the oxygen dissociation curve left, so it is treated with 100 percent oxygen, and hyperbaric oxygen in selected cases; pulse oximetry is misleadingly normal. Methemoglobinemia, with oxidized iron that cannot carry oxygen, causes cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen and chocolate-colored blood; methylene blue reduces it, except in

G6PD deficiency. Iron poisoning is treated with deferoxamine, lead with succimer, calcium disodium EDTA or dimercaprol depending on severity, and arsenic and acute mercury with dimercaprol or related chelators. Digoxin toxicity is treated with digoxin-specific antibody fragments, heparin overdose with protamine, warfarin with vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate, and dabigatran with idarucizumab. Tricyclic antidepressant toxicity with wide QRS is treated with sodium bicarbonate. Beta blocker and calcium channel blocker overdose may need intravenous calcium, glucagon, high-dose insulin and vasopressors. Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia that recurs after dextrose is treated with octreotide. Isoniazid-induced seizures respond to pyridoxine. Local anesthetic systemic toxicity responds to lipid emulsion. Physostigmine can reverse pure anticholinergic delirium but is avoided if tricyclics are involved because of seizure and cardiac risk.

Elimination can be enhanced in selected cases. Activated charcoal binds many drugs if given within about an hour and the airway is protected, but not alcohols, lithium, iron or metals. Urinary alkalinization with bicarbonate traps salicylate ions in urine and is paired with hemodialysis in severe cases. Hemodialysis is considered for lithium, salicylates, toxic alcohols and metformin-associated lactic acidosis.

Worked example: a farmer arrives with salivation, wheeze, bradycardia, pinpoint pupils and fasciculations. This is a cholinergic toxidrome from organophosphate poisoning, and atropine with pralidoxime addresses the muscarinic and nicotinic effects.

lessons.title: Drug Interactions, Pharmacogenomics and Teratogens
body: Drug interactions arise in two ways. Pharmacodynamic interactions occur when drugs act on the same or opposing pathways: additive sedation from opioids with benzodiazepines, additive QT prolongation from several antiarrhythmic, antibiotic and antipsychotic drugs, serotonin syndrome from combined serotonergic agents, hyperkalemia from an ACE inhibitor with a potassium-sparing diuretic, and bleeding from anticoagulants with antiplatelets or NSAIDs. Pharmacokinetic interactions alter absorption, distribution, metabolism or excretion, and the most important involve cytochrome P450 enzymes and drug transporters.

Induction increases enzyme synthesis over days to weeks and lowers substrate levels. Classic inducers: rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, St. John's wort, griseofulvin and chronic heavy alcohol use. They reduce effects of warfarin, oral contraceptives, many antiretrovirals, tacrolimus, cyclosporine and others, so toxicity risk reverses when the inducer is withdrawn. Inhibition acts within days and raises substrate levels. Common inhibitors: azole antifungals, macrolides (clarithromycin and erythromycin more than azithromycin), protease inhibitors and cobicistat, amiodarone, cimetidine, fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin (CYP1A2), grapefruit juice (intestinal CYP3A4), isoniazid and fluoxetine or paroxetine (CYP2D6). Some drugs are prodrugs that need activation (clopidogrel by CYP2C19, codeine by CYP2D6, tamoxifen by CYP2D6), so inhibitors reduce efficacy instead. P-glycoprotein and OATP transporters add more interactions, as with digoxin and statins.

Protein binding displacement rarely matters clinically except for drugs with narrow indices and high binding, and the effect is usually transient. Warfarin is the prototype interaction drug: dietary vitamin K, CYP2C9 inhibitors and antibiotics that alter vitamin K-producing gut flora raise INR, while inducers lower it. Excretion interactions include lithium with NSAIDs, thiazides and ACE inhibitors, probenecid with penicillins, and methotrexate with NSAIDs and penicillins competing for tubular secretion.

Pharmacogenomic variation explains patient-specific effects. CYP2D6 poor metabolizers fail to activate codeine, and ultrarapid metabolizers risk morphine toxicity.
